title: Webhook signature verification uses plain `===` string comparison instead of a timing-safe comparison, across all 4 connector-type branches (GitHub, Jira/Atlassian, Slack, generic) — on endpoints whose own code comment states they are 'UNAUTHENTICATED — security is enforced via connector-specific signature verification'
requirement: CWE-208 Observable Timing Discrepancy; OWASP ASVS 6.2.2
description:
**Checklist row:** §13.1 — Input validation & sanitization / general security hardening of externally-reachable endpoints.
**Files:** `webhook.routes.ts`'s own header comment (lines 1-6) states: "Receives inbound webhook payloads from third-party services (GitHub, Jira, etc.). These endpoints are UNAUTHENTICATED — security is enforced via connector-specific signature verification." `verifyWebhookSignature()` (lines 32-92) implements HMAC-SHA256 verification correctly for all 4 branches (`github`, `jira`/`atlassian`, `slack`, and a generic default) — computing the expected HMAC correctly in every case — but every single comparison uses plain string equality: `return signature === expected;` (lines 49, 61, 78) and `return signature === expected || signature === \`sha256=${expected}\`;` (line 89). None uses `crypto.timingSafeEqual`, even though the exact same platform correctly uses it elsewhere (e.g. `risk-management-service/src/routes/internal-tasks.routes.ts`'s `validateToken()`).
**Root Cause:** The HMAC computation itself was implemented carefully and correctly, but the final comparison step — the part that actually matters for timing-attack resistance — was written with ordinary JavaScript `===`, which short-circuits on the first mismatched byte and is measurably (if subtly) faster to reject an early-byte mismatch than a late one.
**Impact:** Because these endpoints are explicitly unauthenticated by design (per the file's own comment) and rely entirely on signature verification as their sole security boundary, a timing side-channel here is unusually consequential: an attacker with enough network samples to statistically distinguish response-time differences could, in principle, forge a valid signature byte-by-byte without ever knowing the shared secret, and inject a forged webhook payload (fake GitHub/Jira/Slack/generic-connector event) that the platform would treat as genuine — potentially creating fabricated integration evidence or triggering unintended sync/automation actions.
**Claude Fix Prompt:**
In `webhook.routes.ts`, replace every `signature === expected` (and the generic branch's OR) with a length-checked `crypto.timingSafeEqual` comparison, e.g.: `function safeCompare(a: string, b: string): boolean { const bufA = Buffer.from(a); const bufB = Buffer.from(b); return bufA.length === bufB.length && timingSafeEqual(bufA, bufB); }` (importing `timingSafeEqual` from `crypto`, already imported elsewhere in the file via dynamic `import('crypto')`), then use `safeCompare(signature, expected)` in all 4 branches, including the generic branch's two-variant check.

title: Real compliance-mapping endpoint exists but the evidence-detail UI never calls it; only failing controls ever show a name
statusRaw: Re-verified 2026-09-02: the specific claim still holds literally (getIntegrationEvidenceComplianceMapping is defined in integrationHubService.js but still never imported/called in IntegrationEvidenceDetailPage.jsx), but the underlying auditor-facing problem is resolved via a different, real path: a 'Mapped Compliance Controls' table now renders on-screen (added in commit 96d20271, predates this defect) fed by getEvidenceVerdicts()/'/mappings/evidence/:id/verdicts', showing frameworkName/controlStringId/controlTitle for every verdict - PASS and FAIL alike - not just an anonymous count badge. Passing controls do have visible names today.
description:
The backend computes a correct, data-backed control mapping: `vibrantix-connector-service/src/services/ComplianceMappingService.ts::buildComplianceMapping` (lines 249-324) walks `integration_check_master -> ucl_master_v2 -> requirement_ucl_mapping_v2 -> framework_requirements`, correlated with real verdicts, exposed at `GET /integration-evidence/:evidenceId/compliance-mapping` (`integration-evidence.routes.ts:312-409`). A frontend service wrapper exists (`getIntegrationEvidenceComplianceMapping` in `integrationHubService.js`), but `IntegrationEvidenceDetailPage.jsx` never imports or calls it (confirmed via repo-wide grep for `ComplianceMapping` in that file - zero matches). The page only calls `getIntegrationEvidenceRiskMapping`, which surfaces only FAILED/PARTIAL controls in an 'Identified Risks' panel; passing controls are reduced to an anonymous count badge (e.g. '5 checks / 1 failed') with no control names, titles, or framework identifiers ever rendered for passes.

Auditor-facing breakage: even for the one provider (Okta) with real, populated verdicts, an auditor reviewing a piece of PASSING evidence cannot see which specific control(s) it satisfies anywhere in the product UI - only a bare pass/fail count. The only place control names ever appear is the failure table, which is backwards from an audit-evidence standpoint: auditors need to see what evidence proves, not just what it failed to prove.
requirement: ISO 27001:2022 Annex A.5.19 / A.5.20 supplier & integration risk controls; ISO/IEC 27007:2019 §6.3.2 evidence verifiability
